- Legal gender change simplified 2016 (court appearance still required) — resident-facing, climate signal only.
- Detention: placement by ID document gender; trans women placed in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them. Extends to island's jails by national law.
- No island-specific data on detention conditions; the findings are mainland inspections.
- Legal representation thin: no LGBT-friendly lawyer referenced on island; mainland lawyer available.
- National report 2020: rise in homophobic/transphobic attacks 2019, ~1,870 victims vs 1,380 in 2018 — national, combined LGB+trans, not island-specific.
- Healthcare: 2022 regional rights report — lack of self-determination, waiting times, inequitable access by location.
- Youth gender-affirming care: senate passed ban under 18 in May 2024, opposed by government, no update; pediatric society issued guidelines late 2024. Unresolved.
- Social: predominantly Muslim island, written law not the whole picture; one same-sex marriage at a town hall in 2023 after "long and complicated path" — shows formal rights exist but lived friction.
- No island-specific violence data.

Rating considerations per rubric:

The biggest documented exposure: tier-1 style state-imposed universal exposure — custody placement by ID marker, in all-male facilities, with documented persistence of serious violations. But this is a detention exposure, contingent on arrest/detention. For a visitor, the probability of being detained is low absent criminal conduct. Still, it's a documented state-imposed practice applying to any trans person who ends up in custody.

Everyday exposure: anti-discrimination law exists, hate-crime aggravator, no criminalisation of gender expression, no bathroom bans documented, no border friction documented. Legal gender recognition is resident-facing (climate signal). Marriage equality resident-facing.

Social hostility: predominantly Muslim island with conservative social attitudes; documented gap between formal law and lived experience (marriage path complicated). But that's friction/hostility at tier 3 at worst and documented only for one couple. No island violence data.

Violence: national rise in homo/transphobic attacks — national, combined categories, not island-level. Per rule 17/7, limited weight; but it is a documented national trend with recent-ish (2019, reported 2020) data. Dated ~5-6 years.

Healthcare: inequitable access, waiting times; for a visitor, routine care possibly affected. Not catastrophic.

Minors: unresolved under-18 ban — but for a visiting minor, the ban isn't in force (passed senate, opposed by government, no update). Care access for a trans minor travelling: uncertain. Also detention placement rules for a minor travelling with guardian — not documented specifically.

No documented border/document friction: this jurisdiction accepts the visitor's home passport; no documented cases of officials rejecting foreign documents. So entry is not documented as an exposure.

So: combined regime — strong formal legal protections (anti-discrimination, hate crime aggravator, no criminalisation), no documented traveler-facing restrictions at borders or facilities, but a documented severe custody-placement exposure (tier 1 in the state's facilities, extended to island jails by national law), thin local legal recourse, conservative social climate with a documented gap between law and lived experience, and no island-specific violence/enforcement data.
